title: Al-'Adiyat: the chargers
hook: by the panting horses, the human is ungrateful to his Lord (Surah 100)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Qari'ah, the striking, and the scales. Your line was light or heavy. Did you give one ordinary thing a little more weight? Day one hundred seventy-five.

Hear it first. Hooves, pounding. Breath snorting out of a horse's nose in the cold. Sparks where iron shoes strike rock. A cloud of dust at dawn, and a line of riders charging straight into the middle of the enemy. Today's surah opens like the first thirty seconds of a war movie. It's one of the most vivid openings in the Qur'an, and people are always surprised where it lands. After all that thunder, it points at something quiet, something inside every person. Today: Al-'Adiyat, the chargers.
screen: `HOOVES, BREATH, SPARKS, DUST.` → `A CHARGE AT DAWN.` → `THEN SOMETHING QUIET.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred opens with five oaths, all about the war horse. The ones that run panting. The ones that strike sparks. The ones that raid at dawn, raising dust, plunging into the crowd. Al-'adiyat means the runners, the chargers. Then the turn, in Pickthall's words: Lo! man is an ingrate unto his Lord. The word is kanud. The early scholar al-Hasan al-Basri explained it: the one who counts his misfortunes and forgets his blessings. Why horses? Commentators point to what a war horse is: an animal that gives everything for its rider. It runs until it pants, into danger, at dawn, because it was fed and cared for. Loyalty at full speed. And the human, fed and cared for far more, often doesn't even say thank you. The surah goes on: and he is a witness to that himself. Deep down, people know. And he is violent in his love of wealth. Then it reminds us of the day the graves are opened and what's in hearts is brought out. So what's the opposite of kanud? Shukr, gratitude, and gratitude here isn't a feeling you sit with. It moves, like the horses. It shows up in thank-yous said out loud, in giving back, in using a gift for what it was given for. And that ends a week of short, sharp surahs: the elephant, the mocker, time twice over, the race for more, the scales, and now the chargers. Gratitude charges forward.
screen: `FIVE OATHS BY THE WAR HORSE.` · `KANUD — THE UNGRATEFUL.` · `COUNTS MISFORTUNES, FORGETS BLESSINGS.` · `THE HORSE GIVES EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `GRATITUDE CHARGES FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let one person come to mind whom you take for granted. The one who's always there, so you've stopped noticing: a parent, a partner, a friend, the person who cleans your office. Picture one specific thing they do. Let yourself feel how much it would cost if they stopped. Then decide on the words you'll use to thank them today, plainly, out loud or in a message. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Adiyat. The chargers, the war horses running at dawn; the name of Surah one hundred. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude charges forward. Thank someone you took for granted today. Don't wait for the right moment. Charge. Day one hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-'Adiyat in the prayers; its verse on human ingratitude is often quoted in teaching about shukr, gratitude shown in words and in action.

myth: the horses are the oath. the point is the human: ungrateful to his Lord.
the surah says the human is a witness to his own ingratitude
kanud was explained as counting misfortunes and forgetting blessings

fork.setup: the surah swears by war horses charging at dawn. what does it say next?
options: that man is ungrateful to his Lord
that horses are a gift to be cared for
fork.reveal: the thunder lands on something quiet: the human is kanud, ungrateful (100:6). the horse's loyalty is the contrast.

original.note: Arabic: the runners, the chargers; war horses in Surah 100.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about a battle.
what it means: oaths by loyal war horses, set against the human who forgets his blessings.
what a scholar hears: kanud glossed by al-Hasan al-Basri; commentators differ whether the runners are horses or pilgrims' camels; 100:6–8 name ingratitude, self-witness and love of wealth.

sources.quoted: Lo! man is an ingrate unto his Lord

sources.ref: al-Hasan al-Basri on kanud (in Tafsir Ibn Kathir)

notes: Please confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 100:6.
Al-Hasan al-Basri's gloss of kanud is widely cited via Ibn Kathir; paraphrased.
Ali ibn Abi Talib reportedly read al-'adiyat as camels at Hajj; the majority read war horses. Noted in the trapdoor only.
